about: IB Mathematics AA HL: the additional higher level (AHL) statements. AA HL = every statement in data/syllabus.json plus every statement here. Codes are the AA guide's own numbers, which never clash with the SL ones (SL 1.1-1.9, AHL 1.10-1.16 and so on). Content is summarised from the guide; ids are permanent and shared with Wasteland Academy's curriculum map. The tagging rules in data/syllabus.json apply.

statements.title: Counting principles and the binomial theorem for rational indices
statements.content: Counting principles (multiplication and addition rules), permutations and combinations of distinct objects, with arrangements of identical objects and circular arrangements excluded. Extends the binomial theorem to (a + b)^n for rational n, written as a^n(1 + b/a)^n, as an infinite series valid for |b/a| < 1 and used for approximations; proof of the theorem is not required.

statements.title: Partial fractions
statements.content: Split a proper rational expression into partial fractions when the denominator has at most two distinct linear factors (degree of numerator less than that of the denominator). Repeated factors, irreducible quadratic factors and improper fractions are outside this statement; the main use is rearranging integrands in 5.15.

statements.title: Complex numbers in Cartesian form and the complex plane
statements.content: The imaginary unit i with i² = −1, complex numbers in Cartesian form a + bi, and the vocabulary of real part, imaginary part, conjugate, modulus and argument. Includes arithmetic in Cartesian form and representing complex numbers as points or vectors in the complex plane (Argand diagram).

statements.title: Modulus-argument and Euler forms of complex numbers
statements.content: Write complex numbers in modulus-argument form r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r cis θ and Euler form re^(iθ), and convert freely between these and Cartesian form. Carry out sums, products and quotients in any form and interpret them geometrically (multiplying moduli and adding arguments as an enlargement and rotation).

statements.title: Conjugate roots, De Moivre's theorem, powers and roots of complex numbers
statements.content: Non-real roots of polynomial equations with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs. De Moivre's theorem (r cis θ)^n = r^n cis nθ, proved by induction for positive integers n and known to hold more widely, is used for powers, nth roots of complex numbers (including roots of unity) and rational exponents.

statements.title: Proof by induction, by contradiction and by counterexample
statements.content: Proof by mathematical induction (for example sums of series, divisibility, derivatives and complex numbers), proof by contradiction (for example irrationality results and the infinitude of primes), and disproof by a counterexample, where the student must show why the example breaks the statement rather than just stating it.

statements.title: Systems of linear equations in up to three unknowns
statements.content: Solve systems of up to three linear equations in up to three unknowns, both by algebra (elimination or row reduction) and by technology. Decide whether a system has a unique solution, infinitely many (giving the general solution in terms of a parameter) or none (inconsistent); links to intersecting planes in 3.18.

statements.title: Polynomial functions: factor and remainder theorems, sum and product of roots
statements.content: Polynomial functions of any degree: their graphs, zeros, roots and factors; the factor and remainder theorems; and the sum (−aₙ₋₁/aₙ) and product ((−1)ⁿa₀/aₙ) of the roots of a polynomial equation, including equations with complex roots. Only the sum and the product of the roots are listed, not sums of pairwise products.

statements.title: Rational functions with a quadratic numerator or denominator
statements.content: Rational functions with a linear numerator over a quadratic denominator, and with a quadratic numerator over a linear denominator, with the reciprocal function as a special case. Sketches must show every asymptote (vertical, horizontal and oblique) and all axis intercepts.

statements.title: Odd and even functions, inverses with a restricted domain, self-inverse functions
statements.content: Odd functions (f(−x) = −f(x)) and even functions (f(−x) = f(x)), including periodic ones such as sin, cos and tan; finding an inverse function, restricting the domain where needed so that one exists; and self-inverse functions, where f⁻¹ = f.

statements.title: Solving inequalities g(x) ≥ f(x) graphically and analytically
statements.content: Solving inequalities of the form g(x) ≥ f(x) both from graphs and analytically. Algebraic or graphical methods are expected for simple polynomials up to degree 3; technology is used for these and for other functions.

statements.title: Graphs of |f(x)|, f(|x|), 1/f(x), f(ax + b) and [f(x)]²; modulus equations and inequalities
statements.content: Graphs of y = |f(x)|, y = f(|x|), y = 1/f(x), y = f(ax + b) and y = [f(x)]² drawn from the graph of y = f(x); and solving equations and inequalities that involve the modulus, algebraically for simple cases and with technology otherwise.

statements.title: Reciprocal trigonometric ratios, Pythagorean identities and inverse trigonometric functions
statements.content: Defines sec θ, cosec θ and cot θ as the reciprocals of cos θ, sin θ and tan θ, and adds the Pythagorean identities 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ. Covers arcsin x, arccos x and arctan x as functions: their restricted domains, principal-value ranges and graphs.

statements.title: Compound angle identities
statements.content: Compound angle identities for sin(A ± B), cos(A ± B) and tan(A ± B), and the double angle identity for tan. Includes deriving the double angle identities from the compound ones, with a link to De Moivre's theorem.

statements.title: Relationships between trigonometric functions and the symmetry of their graphs
statements.content: Relationships between the trigonometric functions shown by the symmetries of their graphs and the unit circle, such as sin(π − θ) = sin θ, cos(π − θ) = −cos θ and tan(π − θ) = −tan θ. Links to odd and even functions and to compound angles.

statements.title: Vectors: concepts, components and algebra
statements.content: Vectors as directed line segments, written in column form or with base vectors i, j, k. Position and displacement vectors (AB = b − a), sums, differences, scalar multiples, the zero vector, parallel vectors, magnitude, unit vectors and the distance between points, treated both algebraically and geometrically, plus proofs of geometric properties with vectors.

statements.title: The scalar product and the angle between vectors
statements.content: The scalar (dot) product, both in components and as v · w = |v||w| cos θ, and its algebraic properties. Using it to find the angle between vectors and to test for perpendicular vectors (v · w = 0) and parallel vectors (|v · w| = |v||w|).

statements.title: Vector equation of a line in two and three dimensions
statements.content: The vector equation of a line r = a + λb in 2D and 3D, the meaning of the position vector a and direction vector b, and its parametric and Cartesian forms. The angle between two lines from their direction vectors, and simple kinematics with λ as time, b as velocity and |b| as speed.

statements.title: Coincident, parallel, intersecting and skew lines
statements.content: Deciding whether two lines are coincident, parallel, intersecting or skew (non-parallel and non-intersecting, possible only in 3D), and finding the point of intersection when there is one.

statements.title: The vector product
statements.content: The vector (cross) product in components and as v × w = |v||w| sin θ n with n given by the right-hand rule, and its properties: anticommutative, distributive, v × v = 0, and zero for non-zero vectors exactly when they are parallel. Using |v × w| for the area of a parallelogram or triangle.

statements.title: Vector and Cartesian equations of a plane
statements.content: Equations of a plane in vector form r = a + λb + μc (b, c non-parallel vectors in the plane), scalar product form r · n = a · n with normal n, and Cartesian form ax + by + cz = d.

statements.title: Intersections and angles between lines and planes
statements.content: Intersections of a line with a plane, of two planes and of three planes, found by solving equations and interpreted geometrically (a point, a line, a plane, or no intersection), linking to systems of linear equations. The angle between a line and a plane and between two planes.

statements.title: Bayes' theorem
statements.content: Using Bayes' theorem to reverse a conditional probability, with at most three events in the partition, for example in medical testing where a test result is used to update the chance of having a disease. Builds on conditional probability and independence from SL.

statements.title: Discrete and continuous random variables: pdfs, mean, variance, median and mode
statements.content: Variance of discrete random variables, and continuous random variables defined by probability density functions (including piecewise ones) that integrate to 1. Covers the mode and median of a continuous variable, E(X), E(X²), Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² and standard deviation for both types, fair games, and the effect of the linear transformation aX + b.

statements.title: Continuity, differentiability, limits and differentiation from first principles
statements.content: An informal sense of continuity and differentiability at a point (never tested formally), limits as convergence or divergence, and the derivative defined from first principles as the limit of (f(x + h) − f(x))/h, used for polynomials only. Higher derivatives with the notations dⁿy/dxⁿ and f⁽ⁿ⁾(x), including nth-derivative patterns proved by induction.

statements.title: Limits by l'Hôpital's rule or Maclaurin series
statements.content: Limits of quotients f(x)/g(x) as x → a or x → ∞ that give the indeterminate forms 0/0 or ∞/∞, found with l'Hôpital's rule (applied more than once if needed) or by Maclaurin series. Includes the standard result sin θ/θ → 1 as θ → 0 and links to horizontal asymptotes.

statements.title: Implicit differentiation, related rates of change and optimisation
statements.content: Implicit differentiation of relations in x and y, related rates of change linked by the chain rule, and optimisation problems, including cases where the best value is at an endpoint of the domain rather than at a stationary point.

statements.title: Further standard derivatives and integrals
statements.content: Derivatives of tan x, sec x, cosec x, cot x, aˣ, logₐ x, arcsin x, arccos x and arctan x, the matching indefinite integrals (read as a family of curves), and the same results for composites with a linear function. Partial fractions (up to two distinct linear factors) are used to rearrange integrands.

statements.title: Integration by substitution and by parts
statements.content: Integration by substitution beyond the reverse chain rule (the substitution is given unless the integral has the form ∫ k g′(x) f(g(x)) dx), with changed limits for definite integrals. Integration by parts, including repeated use and the cyclic case such as ∫ eˣ sin x dx.

statements.title: Areas against the y-axis and volumes of revolution
statements.content: Areas between a curve and the y-axis over a y-interval, found by integrating x with respect to y. Volumes of solids formed by rotating a region through 2π about the x-axis (V = π∫ y² dx) or the y-axis (V = π∫ x² dy), including regions between two curves and design contexts.

statements.title: First-order differential equations
statements.content: First-order differential equations: numerical solution of dy/dx = f(x, y) by Euler's method with constant step h; exact solution of separable equations (including the logistic equation, using partial fractions), homogeneous equations dy/dx = f(y/x) via y = vx, and linear equations y′ + P(x)y = Q(x) via an integrating factor. Contexts include cooling, population growth and radioactive decay.

statements.title: Maclaurin series
statements.content: Maclaurin series for eˣ, sin x, cos x, ln(1 + x) and (1 + x)ᵖ with p rational, and new series built from these by substitution, multiplication, differentiation and integration. Series can also be developed from a differential equation by repeated differentiation.
